items.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995…
items.q: I’ve been working with another group called Lionel Hampton and the Golden Men of Jazz... James Moody usually on tenor saxophone

ctx.x: And then I’ve been working with another group called Lionel Hampton and the Golden Men of Jazz, which is an eight piece all star group. It changes from time to time but usually it’s Al Grey on trombone, Clark Terry and Harry “Sweets” Edison on trumpets, James Moody usually on tenor saxophone, Grady Tate usually on drums, and Milt Hinton or Jimmy Woode on bass. You know and that’s you say “Golden Men” because we’re all over 60. I think that’s the criteria for being a member of this group. But they do mostly all…

know, he’s still got his big band going. The 29th of this month he’s going to do a gig with his big band. I said, oh, boy, I hope he doesn’t have another one, because we’re supposed to do some things in September. We’re going to a big jazz program at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles and they also are going to honor him again at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C. items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I’ve played a lot of gigs with Moody

ctx.x: Who was the saxophone player — was James Moody on the band when you were there?

No, I wasn’t in the band with James Moody. I’ve played a lot of gigs with Moody, I sure wish he had been there. It was Leo Wright, an alto player that’s passed away also, a young alto player originally from Texas but he lived in Germany a great part of his life. He was stationed in the Army there. And then when he finished his Army duty he just stayed there and married and had a family. But he came back after that, and that’s when he joined Dizzy. Before that there was no saxophone player, it was Les Spann…
Were you able, as a member of that group, were you paid per gig or were you on a salary type.
